name: Classical India
title: Social Hierarchy of Classical India: From King to Enslaved
period: c. 320 BCE – 550 CE (the Maurya and Gupta empires)

tiers.name: The king
tiers.you: You rule with a council of ministers and a standing army, take a share of every harvest and are expected to protect your subjects and the order of the varnas, while your sons govern provinces for you.
tiers.kid: Indian kings took part of every harvest as tax and were expected to protect their people.
tiers.rise: Kingship was meant for Kshatriyas, but few dynasties of the age were Kshatriyas by birth: the Nandas were said to be Shudras, the Shungas and Kanvas were Brahmins, and the Gupta records never name their varna. From the 4th century Brahmins gave rising dynasties Kshatriya standing by tracing their descent to the solar and lunar lines of the epics.
tiers.why: The law books made kingship the duty of a Kshatriya: to protect his subjects, punish wrongdoers and uphold the order of the varnas, in return for a share of the harvest, traditionally a sixth.

tiers.name: Brahmins
tiers.you: You were born a Brahmin: you study the Vedas, perform rites for others and live on their gifts, and a king may grant you the revenue of a village, free of tax.
tiers.kid: Brahmins were priests and teachers who learned the holy texts called the Vedas by heart.
tiers.rise: In the law books Brahmin rank came by birth alone. A Brahmin in hard times was allowed to live by a Kshatriya’s or a Vaishya’s work, and one who committed a grievous sin could be cast out of his varna.
tiers.why: The Brahmanical texts placed Brahmins first.

tiers.name: Buddhist and Jain monks and nuns
tiers.you: You have left your family, shaved your head and taken the robe; you own little more than your robes and an alms bowl, eat only before noon and live by the rules of your order.
tiers.kid: Buddhist and Jain monks and nuns gave up their homes to live simply and study their faith.
tiers.rise: Anyone free of debt and servitude could take the robe, whatever their varna, and a monk or nun could leave the order and return to household life.
tiers.why: Buddhist and Jain monks and nuns, and the ascetics of smaller orders such as the Ajivikas, left household life and stood outside the varna order: the Buddhist order took people of every varna, though not slaves or…

tiers.name: Kshatriyas
tiers.you: You were born to a warrior lineage: the law books tell you to fight, govern and protect, to study the Vedas and give gifts, and you may command troops or govern a province.
tiers.kid: Kshatriyas were warriors and rulers whose duty was to protect the people.
tiers.rise: Kshatriya rank came by birth, but success could claim it: from the 4th century Brahmins gave newly risen royal families Kshatriya genealogies, while a Kshatriya people that abandoned the rites could be counted as fallen.
tiers.why: The Kshatriyas were the warrior and ruling varna.

tiers.name: Vaishyas
tiers.you: You trade or lend money, belong to a guild that has its own laws and takes deposits, and as one of the twice-born you may study the Vedas.
tiers.kid: Vaishyas were traders, bankers and farmers, and many of them belonged to guilds.
tiers.rise: The varna came by birth, but trade could make a family rich and powerful: guild heads sat on councils and advised kings, and some historians think the Gupta dynasty itself was of Vaishya origin.
tiers.why: The Vaishyas were the third varna and, like the two above them, twice-born, entitled to study the Vedas.

tiers.name: Shudras
tiers.you: You farm, labour or work at a craft; the law books say you were born to serve the twice-born and may not study the Vedas, but they leave you freer of their ritual rules.
tiers.kid: Shudras were farmers, workers and craftspeople, and old law books said they should serve the higher groups.
tiers.rise: Birth fixed the varna in the texts, but some Shudras grew rich and powerful, and an outcaste group that took up farming could be absorbed into the Shudras.
tiers.why: The Shudras were the fourth varna, born, the law books said, to serve the three twice-born varnas.

tiers.name: Chandalas and other outcastes
tiers.you: You live outside the village, carry away the dead or hunt and fish for a living, and when you enter a town or a market you must strike a piece of wood so that others can avoid your touch.
tiers.kid: Chandalas were made to live apart from others and did work such as carrying away the dead.
tiers.rise: The texts made the status hereditary, but over generations groups could move: a forest people that settled to farming could be absorbed among the Shudras.
tiers.why: Below and outside the four varnas the texts placed groups they held to be impure, above all the Chandalas, along with the Shvapachas and peoples such as the Nishadas.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were captured in war, born in the house or bought; you serve your owner’s household, but you may keep what you earn and, if you can pay your price, buy back your freedom.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay, often as servants in homes.
tiers.rise: Freedom came by the owner’s grant or by paying one’s price, a right the Arthashastra recognised; a free man pledged for a debt was released when it was repaid.
tiers.why: Slavery existed throughout these centuries, but historians such as Romila Thapar note that slaves were not the main labour force, as they were in Greece; most served in households as servants, nurses and attendants…
